lesson.title: Where the Bend Switches Direction: Finding True Inflection Points
lesson.summary: Solving f''(x) = 0 only produces a candidate inflection point; confirming that concavity actually reverses sign there is what makes it genuine, the same necessary but not sufficient caution that governs critical numbers.
lesson.body:
An inflection point is a point where a graph's concavity actually changes, from concave up to concave down or the reverse. Inflection analysis is the full procedure for finding these points with certainty: solve f''(x) = 0 (or locate where f'' is undefined) to get candidate locations, and then confirm each candidate by checking that concavity genuinely reverses sign there. That second step is not optional, as the next example shows.

Continuing the running example, concavity analysis already found that f(x) = 2x^3 - 3x^2 - 12x + 5 has f''(x) = 12x - 6, equal to zero at x = 1/2, with concavity switching from negative to positive right there. That sign change is exactly what confirms a genuine inflection point. Its height is f(1/2) = 2(1/8) - 3(1/4) - 12(1/2) + 5 = 0.25 - 0.75 - 6 + 5 = -1.5, so the inflection point sits at (0.5, -1.5).

Now consider a case where solving f''(x) = 0 gives a false alarm. Let g(x) = x^4. Then g'(x) = 4x^3 and g''(x) = 12x^2, so g''(x) = 0 at x = 0. But test the sign on both sides: at x = -1, g''(-1) = 12, positive, and at x = 1, g''(1) = 12, also positive. The concavity never actually changes, g stays concave up on both sides of x = 0, it just flattens for an instant. So x = 0 is not an inflection point, even though it correctly solves f''(x) = 0. This mirrors the caution from local extrema analysis, where solving f'(x) = 0 did not guarantee an extremum either. In both cases, solving an equation only produces a candidate. Confirming an actual sign change is what makes it real.

Beyond curve sketching, inflection points mark where the rate of curving reverses, which has a direct practical reading: on a curve that rises while concave up, growth is accelerating, and once it crosses an inflection point into concave down territory, growth is still happening but is now decelerating. The inflection point itself is where growth was fastest. That framing, watching not just what a quantity does but how the speed of the change itself is changing, becomes genuinely useful once real optimization scenarios are on the table.

With local extrema, concavity, and inflection points all mapped out for a function, you now have every piece needed to sketch its graph accurately from the algebra alone. That same toolkit, critical numbers, sign charts, and the discipline of confirming a candidate before trusting it, is exactly what carries forward into optimization, where the function you are analyzing usually is not handed to you ready made, but has to be built first from a real world description.
